title: Episode 165: Woodrow Wilson and the Road to War: Lusitania, Zimmerman, and the Great Crusade (1914–1917)
description:
When the guns of August 1914 plunged Europe into the horrific slaughter of World War I, President Woodrow Wilson issued an urgent plea to the American people: 'We must be impartial in thought, as well as action.' For nearly three agonizing years, Wilson walked a precarious diplomatic tightrope, resisting furious war hawks led by Theodore Roosevelt after a German submarine torpedoed the British ocean liner Lusitania, killing 128 Americans. Re-elected in 1916 on the proud slogan 'He Kept Us Out of War,' Wilson was soon confronted by Imperial Germany's declaration of unrestricted submarine warfare and the shocking intercepted Zimmerman Telegram proposing a Mexican invasion of Texas. Discover the agonizing moral journey that led Wilson to call America to arms to make the world safe for democracy.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the crucible of the First World War alongside Woodrow Wilson. A devout pacifist scholar who detested bloodshed, Wilson struggled for three long years to keep the United States neutral while Europe tore itself to pieces in the mud of the Western Front. Yet when Imperial Germany unleashed its submarine wolfpacks and plotted against American soil, Wilson made the fateful decision that thrust the United States into global war. Here is George with the full story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: NEUTRALITY IN THOUGHT AND ACTION
In August 1914, as millions of soldiers marched across Europe to the roar of artillery, Woodrow Wilson sat in the White House mourning the death of his beloved wife Ellen. Grief-stricken and physically exhausted, Wilson watched with horror as western civilization seemed to tear itself apart in the opening battles of the Great War. America was a nation of immigrants: one-third of the population had been born in Europe or had immigrant parents. Millions of German Americans sympathized with the Fatherland, millions of Irish Americans despised Great Britain, while Anglo-Saxon elites in Boston and New York cheered passionately for the Allies.\n\nWilson understood that if the American government took sides, the domestic fabric of the Republic would fracture into violent ethnic strife. On August 19, 1914, Wilson issued a solemn proclamation to the American people: 'The United States must be neutral in fact, as well as in name, during these days that are to try men's souls. We must be impartial in thought, as well as action, must put a curb upon our sentiments.' For two years, Wilson offered his services as an impartial mediator, urging European monarchs and prime ministers to conclude a 'peace without victory'—a settlement that would punish no one and leave no bitter grievances to fester into future conflicts. Wilson recognized that neutrality in thought and deed was nearly impossible in a global conflict that threatened the freedom of the high seas and the safety of peaceful merchant vessels. Wilson understood that modern warfare was no longer a contest of gallant armies, but a total struggle that demanded the complete mobilization of American industry, agriculture, and civic willpower.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE SINKING OF THE LUSITANIA
The illusion of peaceful neutrality was shattered on May 7, 1915. Off the Old Head of Kinsale on the southern coast of Ireland, the German submarine U-20 spotted the British luxury ocean liner RMS Lusitania through its periscope. Kapitänleutnant Walther Schwieger fired a single torpedo into the starboard bow. A catastrophic secondary explosion—likely caused by coal dust or four million rounds of hidden American rifle ammunition in the cargo hold—ripped the hull open. In just eighteen minutes, the giant four-funneled liner plunged beneath the waves, taking 1,198 civilian lives, including 128 American citizens and 94 small children.\n\nAmerica erupted in furious outrage. Former President Theodore Roosevelt denounced the sinking as an act of mass murder and piracy, demanding an immediate declaration of war against Imperial Germany and mocking Wilson's restraint. But Wilson refused to be rushed into slaughter: 'There is such a thing as a man being too proud to fight,' Wilson declared in a famous Philadelphia speech. 'There is such a thing as a nation being so right that it does not need to convince others by force that it is right.' Wilson dispatched a series of stern diplomatic notes to Berlin demanding an apology, financial reparations, and a pledge to cease attacking unarmed passenger ships without warning. Fearing American entry, the German Kaiser backed down, issuing the 'Arabic Pledge' to restrict submarine warfare. The sinking of the Lusitania brought home the horrifying reality of unrestricted submarine warfare, shocking the conscience of a nation that had previously viewed the European conflict as a distant tragedy. The loss of one hundred and twenty-eight American lives aboard the Lusitania permanently transformed public sentiment, making neutrality an increasingly untenable fiction.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: 'HE KEPT US OUT OF WAR'
In 1916, Wilson faced a formidable challenge for reelection from Republican nominee Charles Evans Hughes, a distinguished Supreme Court Justice and former governor of New York. While Hughes struggled to balance the demands of hawkish pro-war Republicans under Theodore Roosevelt with pacifist German American voters in the Midwest, the Democratic Party rallied behind a singular, electrifying slogan: 'He Kept Us Out of War!'\n\nWilson himself was deeply uneasy with the slogan, knowing that events beyond the Atlantic might easily force his hand: 'I can't keep the country out of war,' Wilson privately warned an aide. 'Any little German lieutenant can push us into war at any time by sinking a ship.' On election night, early returns from New York and the East Coast heavily favored Hughes; newspapers declared Hughes the victor, and Hughes went to bed believing he was President. But as returns trickled in from the Pacific Coast and the rural western states, working-class farmers and newly enfranchised women voters in California, Washington, and Ohio swung overwhelmingly for Wilson. Wilson carried California by just 3,773 votes, securing 277 electoral votes to Hughes's 254. The peace president had won a second term. Despite the immense political pressure for war from bellicose figures like Theodore Roosevelt, Wilson stubbornly pursued peaceful diplomatic remedies to protect American honor without rushing into armed conflict. His patient, agonizing correspondence with Berlin bought precious months for American factories and shipyards to prepare for the conflict that was becoming inevitable.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE GERMAN GAMBLE: UNRESTRICTED SUBMARINE WARFARE
By January 1917, the European battlefields had become slaughterhouses of unimaginable scale. At Verdun and the Somme, over one million young men had died in the mud for gains measured in yards. British naval blockades were starving the German home front, forcing German civilians to survive on turnips and saw-dust bread during the bitter 'Turnip Winter.' In Berlin, Imperial German military commanders Field Marshal Paul von Hindenburg and General Erich Ludendorff made a desperate, fateful decision.\n\nThey calculated that if Germany's fleet of two hundred modern U-boats were unleashed to sink all merchant shipping approaching Great Britain without warning, Britain would be starved into total surrender within five months—long before the tiny, unprepared United States Army could train, equip, and transport an expeditionary force across the Atlantic. On January 31, 1917, the German ambassador in Washington walked into the State Department and handed Secretary of State Robert Lansing an official diplomatic notice: at midnight, Germany would resume unrestricted submarine warfare across the entire Atlantic. Wilson was crushed; the German government had deliberately torn up its pledges. On February 3, Wilson severed formal diplomatic relations with Germany. The slogan 'He Kept Us Out of War' captured the deep yearning of everyday Americans for peace, securing Wilson's narrow re-election in one of the closest contests in presidential history. The 1916 election highlighted the deep cultural divide between the interventionist Northeast and the determinedly neutral agricultural heartland of the Midwest and West.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: ROOM 40 AND THE ZIMMERMAN TELEGRAM
Just as Wilson hesitated on the brink of war, an explosive piece of intelligence arrived from London. In January 1917, British naval cryptanalysts operating in the top-secret 'Room 40' had intercepted and decoded an encrypted telegram sent from German Foreign Minister Arthur Zimmermann to the German minister in Mexico City. The telegram contained an astonishing, audacious proposal:\n\nIf the United States entered the war against Germany, Germany proposed a military alliance with Mexico. Germany would provide unlimited financial and military support, and in return, Mexico would invade the southwestern United States and conquer its 'lost territory' in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. Furthermore, the Mexican president was urged to invite the Japanese Empire to switch sides and attack California. On February 24, the British government handed the decoded transcript to American Ambassador Walter Hines Page. When Wilson read the message, he was thunderstruck by Germany's sheer treachery. On March 1, Wilson released the Zimmerman Telegram to the American press, igniting a tidal wave of outrage across the American South and West. The intercept and publication of the Zimmerman Telegram shattered any remaining illusions of German goodwill, uniting the American heartland behind the defense of the nation's territorial integrity. The Zimmerman Telegram revealed a breathtaking geopolitical conspiracy that brought the reality of global war directly to the borders of Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE ADDRESS TO CONGRESS: APRIL 2, 1917
Throughout late March 1917, German U-boats torpedoed five American merchant vessels in rapid succession, killing dozens of American sailors. The Russian Revolution had overthrown the Tsarist autocracy in March, removing the moral stain of allied partnership with a Russian despot and framing the global struggle cleanly as democracy against autocracy. Wilson spent long, solitary nights walking the White House corridors, wrestling with the terrible burden of sending hundreds of thousands of young American boys to their deaths.\n\nOn the evening of April 2, 1917, a heavy spring rain fell on Washington as cavalry escorts with drawn sabers accompanied the President's carriage to Capitol Hill. Standing before a joint session of Congress, illuminated by incandescent chandeliers, Woodrow Wilson delivered one of the most famous addresses in human history. His voice was quiet, solemn, and morally terrifying in its clarity:\n\n'It is a fearful thing to lead this great peaceful people into war, into the most terrible and disastrous of all wars, civilization itself seeming to be in the balance. But the right is more precious than peace, and we shall fight for the things which we have always carried nearest our hearts—for democracy, for the right of those who submit to authority to have a voice in their own Governments, for the rights and liberties of small nations, for a universal dominion of right by such a concert of free peoples as shall bring peace and safety to all nations and make the world itself at last free. To such a task we can dedicate our lives and our fortunes... The world must be made safe for democracy.' That historic war address before Congress framed the American intervention in noble, selfless terms: fighting not for conquest or dominion, but for the universal triumph of human freedom and democracy. Standing before Congress that April night, Wilson delivered one of the most consequential addresses in the history of the republic, leading a peace-loving nation into a crusade for global democracy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE TEARS IN THE OVAL OFFICE
When Wilson concluded his address, the House chamber erupted in deafening, sustained thunder. Senators waved miniature American flags, congressmen stood on their desks shouting approval, and Chief Justice Edward Douglass White wept openly with emotion. Four days later, on Good Friday, April 6, 1917, Congress formally declared war against Imperial Germany. The American Republic had entered the First World War.\n\nYet when Wilson returned to the White House that evening, there was no celebration. Entering his private office with his secretary Joseph Tumulty, Wilson sat down at his mahogany desk, placed his face in his hands, and wept like a child. 'Think of what it was they were applauding,' Wilson whispered to Tumulty with agonizing sorrow. 'My message today was a message of death for our young men. How strange it seems to applaud that.' Two million American doughboys would cross the submarine-infested Atlantic to fight in the trenches of France. Woodrow Wilson had launched the greatest moral crusade in American history, embarking on a path that would win the war, reshape the global order, and ultimately break his own heart and body. In taking up the sword of democracy, Woodrow Wilson summoned the immense industrial and human energy of the United States to decide the fate of modern European civilization. The entry of the United States tipped the scales of world conflict decisively, ensuring that democratic ideals would prevail over imperial autocracy.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Woodrow Wilson's decision to enter World War I transformed the United States into the decisive military and moral arbiter of the twentieth century. His soaring vision of a war to end all wars established an enduring ideal of global democracy. Next week, we examine Wilson's triumph and tragedy at the Paris Peace Conference: the Fourteen Points, the birth of the League of Nations, and the catastrophic physical collapse that cut short his final crusade. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
